content: Children who consumed meat three or more times per week had a significantly higher prevalence of being underweight compared to those who never consumed meat. However, no difference in underweight prevalence was observed between children consuming meat three or more times per week and those consuming meat one to two times per week. Interestingly, children who consumed meat one to two times per week had a significantly higher risk of being underweight compared to those who never consumed meat, although the certainty of this evidence was graded as very low. Zhao et al. (2016) evaluated underweight prevalence in children aged 6 to 36 months, comparing those who consumed any meat to those who consumed no meat. They found no significant difference in underweight prevalence between the two groups, with the evidence graded as very low. Urkin et al. (2007) reported on anemia in children but were unable to provide measurable outcomes due to missing data. They defined higher meat consumption as four times per week and lower consumption as zero to three times per week, using a non-comparative prospective study design. Silva et al. (2007) assessed anemia (hemoglobin <11 g/dL) in children aged 6 to 12 months who consumed red meat. A potential reduction in anemia was observed in children consuming red meat daily or weekly compared to those consuming it less than weekly. Additionally, children who consumed red meat in the past 24 hours had a significantly lower risk of anemia compared to those who did not, although the evidence was graded as very low. Silva et al. also evaluated the impact of liver consumption on anemia in children aged 6 to 12 months. No significant differences in anemia prevalence were found between children consuming liver daily or weekly and those consuming it less than weekly. Similarly, no differences were observed between children who consumed liver in the past 24 hours and those who did not, with the evidence graded as very low. Ahmad et al. (2018) and Zhao et al. (2016) assessed the impact of egg consumption on stunting, wasting, and underweight in children. No significant differences in stunting, wasting, or underweight were observed between children consuming eggs at varying frequencies (≥4 times/week, 1–3 times/week, or never). The evidence for these outcomes was graded as very low. Ahmad et al. (2018) also evaluated fish consumption in children aged 6 to 23 months. No significant differences in stunting or underweight were observed between children consuming fish at different frequencies. However, a significant 48% reduction in wasting was reported among children consuming fish four or more times per week compared to those consuming fish one to three times per week, with the evidence graded as very low. Engelmann et al. (1998) assessed the impact of meat consumption (beef, pork, lamb, turkey, and/or cod) on growth and nutritional outcomes in children aged 8 to 10 months. No significant differences were observed in height, weight, triceps skinfold thickness, hemoglobin concentration, serum ferritin levels, transferrin receptor levels, or zinc intake between children consuming 27 g/day of meat and those consuming 10 g/day of meat. The evidence for these outcomes was graded as very low. Krebs et al. (2012) evaluated the effects of lyophilized beef consumption on stunting, wasting, weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ), height-for-age z-scores (HAZ), weight-for-height z-scores (WHZ), head circumference-for-age z-scores (HCAZ), vitamin B12 levels, transferrin receptor levels, and zinc intake in children aged 9 to 18 months. No significant differences were observed in most outcomes between children consuming higher amounts of lyophilized beef (30–45 g/day) and those consuming lesser amounts (70–105 kcal/day of cereal). However, children consuming higher amounts of lyophilized beef had significantly lower mean WAZ and HCAZ compared to those consuming lesser amounts, with the evidence graded as low. Tang et al. (2014) assessed the impact of pork consumption on growth outcomes in children aged 6 to 18 months. Children consuming 60 g of pork daily had significantly higher WAZ, HAZ, and head circumference changes compared to those consuming no pork and eating cereals daily. However, no significant differences were observed in WHZ or weight changes. The evidence for these outcomes was graded as moderate. Iannotti et al. (2017) and Stewart et al. (2019) evaluated the impact of egg consumption on WAZ, HAZ, and WHZ in children aged 6 to 9 months. Children consuming one egg per day for six months showed no significant differences in these outcomes compared to those who did not consume eggs. The evidence for these outcomes was graded as low.
